title: Template Argument Deduction
learning_outcomes: Describe when template argument deduction is useful and what problem it does not solve.
Evaluate a small example against its stated constraints, standard version and implementation assumptions.
Select a test or tool that can provide evidence of correctness without treating one successful run as proof.

content.intro: Template Argument Deduction focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.
content.why_it_matters: Template Argument Deduction matters because test templates with multiple types and choose constraints that state the operations the implementation actually needs. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Generic programming describes reusable operations in terms of requirements on types. Concepts and constraints make those requirements more visible at the interface.

Template Argument Deduction focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.

Test templates with multiple types and choose constraints that state the operations the implementation actually needs.

content_blocks.title: Minimal example: Template Argument Deduction
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `example.cpp`. Compile using `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic example.cpp -o example; then run ./example (Windows: .\example.exe).` The CodeLeaf page shows reference output only; it does not execute C++ learner code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the example, rebuild with the same standard and warning flags, and rerun the same input. If the example is nondeterministic or depends on platform support, record that constraint instead of expecting byte-for-byte identical output.
content_blocks.limitations: The built-in CodeLeaf page does not execute C++ in a sandbox. Compile local teaching examples only; arbitrary learner code requires a separately deployed isolated runner with CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network limits.
content_blocks.explanation: Class template argument deduction can infer template arguments from constructor arguments. Do not rely on deduction when explicit types make intent clearer.

items.title: Function Template Deduction
items.text: Templates describe families of functions or types instantiated for specific template arguments; errors may appear during instantiation.

items.title: Class Template Argument Deduction (C++17)
items.text: Templates describe families of functions or types instantiated for specific template arguments; errors may appear during instantiation.

items.title: Deduction Guides
items.text: GUI systems are commonly event-driven and impose thread-affinity and lifecycle rules; concrete examples require the selected GUI toolkit.

items.title: Explicit Template Arguments
items.text: Explain explicit template arguments in the context of Template Argument Deduction: identify the rule, trace a minimal example, and check one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Deduction and References
items.text: A reference aliases an existing object and must not outlive that object; references are not reseatable after initialization.

items.title: Common Deduction Failures
items.text: Identify how common deduction failures can fail, what diagnostic evidence to collect, and which validation or design choice reduces the risk.

content_blocks.title: Guided practice
content_blocks.text: Before changing the example, predict the output and name the rule that produces it. Then modify one line to demonstrate function template deduction, and add a test for one boundary or failure scenario. Keep the experiment small enough that another learner can reproduce it.

content_blocks.title: Version, safety and portability note
content_blocks.text: This topic may depend on newer C++ language or library support; this example uses a C++20-compatible illustration. Feature support varies by compiler version and standard-library implementation. Check the references and prefer explicit diagnostics to assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
